english: Did you take attendance / has it been called?
usage: Polite; ask a classmate if attendance was already taken
반말, to a classmate you're friendly with
출석 체크 = 'attendance check', the everyday phrasing
아직 ('yet') when you're checking you didn't miss it
examples: 출석 불렀어요?
Did they take attendance?
Whispered to the person next to you as you arrive
저 늦었는데 출석 불렀어요?
I'm late — did they already call roll?
저 늦었는데 ('I'm late, so…') sets up the worry
선생님, 저 왔어요. 출석 좀 체크해 주세요.
Teacher, I'm here. Please mark me present.
출석 체크해 주세요 to the teacher when you arrived late
nuance: 출석 불렀어요? is 출석 ('attendance', Sino-Korean 出席) + 불렀어요 (past of 부르다 'to call'). Calling roll is literally 출석을 부르다 ('to call attendance'), so this asks 'have they called the roll yet?' — the thing a latecomer most wants to know. It's the polite -어요 form you'd use with a classmate you don't know well; with a friend it drops to 출석 불렀어?. The everyday near-synonym is 출석 체크했어요? (출석 + the loanword 체크 'check'), which is interchangeable in casual academy talk. The key contrast is direction: 출석 불렀어요? asks a peer whether it happened, while 출석 체크해 주세요 asks the TEACHER to mark you present — don't say 출석 불러 주세요 to mean 'mark me', because 부르다 means the act of reading names aloud, not recording you. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'take attendance' word-for-word with 가지다 ('to take/hold') — 출석을 가져요 is meaningless; Korean uses 부르다 ('call') or 체크하다. Also note 출석 is the opposite of 결석 ('absence'); don't mix them up.

Confusing 출석 with 출근.
출석 is attendance at class/school; 출근 is 'going to work / clocking in.' Say 출석 for the classroom, not 출근.

english: I won't be coming to class today
usage: Polite; telling the teacher you can't come
반말, to a classmate, not the teacher
수업 못 듣다 ('can't take the class') variant
examples: 선생님, 저 오늘 결석할게요.
Teacher, I'll be absent today.
A heads-up message before class starts
몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요. 죄송합니다.
I'm not feeling well, so I'll miss today. Sorry.
Give a reason (몸이 안 좋다) then apologize
내일 일이 생겨서 결석하게 됐어요. 미리 말씀드려요.
Something came up tomorrow so I'll be absent. Telling you in advance.
결석하게 됐어요 ('it turned out I'll be absent') sounds less willful
nuance: 오늘 결석할게요 is 오늘 ('today') + 결석 ('absence', Sino-Korean 缺席) + -할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 ending that announces your own intention as a courteous notice). It's how you tell a teacher or academy you won't attend. Register matters a lot here: to the teacher you keep -할게요 or go more formal, and you almost always add a reason + 죄송합니다, because announcing an absence bluntly can feel rude. The softer, blame-deflecting variant is 결석하게 됐어요 ('it came to be that I'll be absent'), which frames it as circumstance, not choice — very useful for sounding polite. The everyday plain alternative is 오늘 못 가요 ('I can't come today'). The contrast to watch: 결석 is the neutral/formal word for a missed class, while 빠지다 ('to skip/drop out of') as in 오늘 수업 빠질게요 is more casual and can hint you're choosing to skip — fine with friends, a bit loose to a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'be absent' tempts 있다/없다, but you cannot say 결석이에요 for a planned absence to the teacher; use the verb 결석하다. Also avoid 'skip class' as 점프하다 (a 직역 trap) — that's nonsense in Korean.

직역 of 'skip/jump' doesn't work. Korean uses 결석하다 (formal) or 수업 빠지다 (casual): 오늘 수업 빠질게요.
Announcing the absence with no reason or apology.
A bare 결석할게요 can sound abrupt to a teacher. Add a reason and 죄송합니다: 몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요, 죄송합니다.

usage: Polite; ask the teacher or a classmate
Checking whether any was assigned at all
Asking the range/how much (어디까지 = 'up to where')
examples: 숙제가 뭐예요?
What's the homework?
Asked at the end of class or to a friend later
오늘 숙제 있어요? 있으면 뭐예요?
Is there homework today? If so, what is it?
Two-step: check existence, then content
저 어제 결석해서 그런데, 숙제가 뭐였어요?
I was absent yesterday — what was the homework?
Past 뭐였어요 for homework already assigned
nuance: 숙제가 뭐예요? is 숙제 ('homework', Sino-Korean 宿題) + 가 (subject particle) + 뭐예요 ('what is it?'). It's the basic ask for an assignment, fine to the teacher or a classmate. 숙제 is the standard schoolwork word; in a university/academy context you'll also hear 과제 ('assignment/task', 課題), which sounds more formal and is used for bigger projects, essays, and reports, whereas 숙제 is everyday practice work — using 숙제 for a major term paper sounds a little childish, and 과제 for tiny daily exercises sounds stiff, so match the size of the task. A frequent practical variant is 숙제 어디까지예요? ('how far does the homework go?'), since Korean classes often assign by page range. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: many learners drop it or use 을/를 (숙제를 뭐예요 is wrong) — with 뭐예요 you use the subject 가, or just drop the particle in speech (숙제 뭐예요?). Another trap is treating 숙제 as a verb; it's a noun, so 'do homework' is 숙제하다 / 숙제를 하다, not 숙제다. If you missed a day, switch to past tense: 숙제가 뭐였어요?

examples: 숙제 언제까지예요?
When's the homework due?
Asked right after homework is assigned
이 과제 언제까지 내야 돼요?
By when do I have to submit this assignment?
내야 돼요 ('have to submit') makes the duty explicit
다음 주 월요일까지예요? 아니면 수업 전까지예요?
Is it due next Monday, or before class?
Pinning down the exact cutoff with 까지
nuance: 숙제 언제까지예요? is 숙제 + 언제 ('when') + 까지 ('until/by') + 예요. The particle 까지 is doing the heavy lifting: it means 'by (a deadline)', so 언제까지 = 'by when'. This is the natural way to ask a due date, far more idiomatic than 언제 ('when') alone — 숙제 언제예요? sounds like asking when homework happens, not when it's due, so 까지 is essential. For formal assignments the word 마감 ('deadline', lit. 'closing') appears: 과제 마감 언제예요?. The contrast to know: -까지 means 'by/up to and including that point' (a deadline you must meet), while -까지는 or 동안 ('during') express duration — don't confuse 'due by Monday' (월요일까지) with 'until Monday' in the sense of an ongoing period. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 까지 and just asking 언제 (which loses the 'deadline' sense), or using 'submit' as 제출하다 in casual speech when 내다 ('to hand in') is more natural: 언제까지 내야 돼요?. Also, 'due' has no single Korean word — you express it with 까지 + 내다/제출하다, not a 직역.

usage: Polite; reporting to the teacher you're done
끝내다 ('to finish/complete') for a bigger task
I haven't done the homework yet
The honest opposite, with 아직 + 못
examples: 숙제 다 했어요.
I finished the homework.
Said when the teacher checks who's done
숙제 다 했는데 하나는 모르겠어요.
I did all of it, but one I couldn't figure out.
다 했는데 ('I did it all, but…') flags a question
죄송해요, 숙제 다 못 했어요. 시간이 없었어요.
Sorry, I didn't finish the homework. I ran out of time.
다 못 했어요 ('couldn't finish it all') to confess politely
nuance: 숙제 다 했어요 is 숙제 + 다 ('all') + 했어요 (past of 하다 'to do'). The little word 다 means 'all/completely' and is what turns 'I did homework' into 'I finished it all' — it's the natural completion marker, more idiomatic than 완성했어요 ('completed', which sounds like finishing a painting or building) for everyday homework. The negative is the crucial pair: 'I didn't do it' splits into 안 했어요 (didn't do it — chose not to / just didn't) vs. 못 했어요 (couldn't do it — tried but failed / had no time). To a teacher, 다 못 했어요 ('couldn't finish') sounds more sympathetic than 안 했어요 ('didn't do it'), so pick deliberately. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 안/못 distinction: saying 숙제 안 했어요 when you mean you ran out of time makes you sound like you blew it off. Another trap is placing 다 wrong — it goes before the verb (다 했어요), not after. For a major 과제, 끝냈어요 ('finished/wrapped up') sounds better than 했어요.

english: Could you explain it once more?
usage: Polite; ask the teacher to repeat
반말, to a classmate helping you
Add 천천히 ('slowly') when you can't keep up
examples: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요.
Please explain it once more.
Raise your hand and say this when lost
죄송한데 이 부분 한 번 더 설명해 주세요.
Sorry, could you explain this part again?
이 부분 ('this part') points to exactly where
이해가 잘 안 돼서 천천히 한 번 더 설명해 주실 수 있어요?
I don't quite get it — could you explain slowly once more?
이해가 안 돼서 ('because I don't understand') gives the reason
nuance: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 is 한 번 ('one time') + 더 ('more') + 설명하다 ('to explain', 說明) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The favor verb 주세요 is essential — it asks the teacher to explain FOR your benefit, which is polite; bare 설명하세요 would be an order ('you, explain!') and sounds rude to a teacher. 한 번 더 ('one more time') is the crisp, natural way to ask for a repeat; the near-synonym 다시 ('again') also works (다시 설명해 주세요), the difference being that 한 번 더 stresses 'one additional time' while 다시 stresses 'from the start/over again' — both fine in class. To sound more deferential to a teacher you respect, swap 말하다 for the humble-honorific 말씀하다: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?. The English-speaker pitfall is omitting 주다 and commanding 설명하세요, or 직역-ing 'one more time' as 한 더 번 (wrong order — the counter sequence is number + 번, so 한 번 + 더). Also, to say you didn't understand, use 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't get understood'), not 나는 이해하지 않아요, which sounds like you refuse to understand.

Saying 이해하지 않아요 for 'I don't understand'.
That sounds like 'I refuse to understand.' Natural Korean is 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood') or 잘 모르겠어요.

usage: Polite; flag that you want to ask
Softer opener with -는데요, invites the teacher to respond
여쭤보다 (humble 'ask') to a teacher, very polite
examples: 선생님, 질문 있어요.
Teacher, I have a question.
Raise your hand and lead with this
여기 질문 있는데요, 이거 왜 이렇게 돼요?
I have a question here — why does it become like this?
질문 있는데요 then ask the actual 왜 ('why')
수업 끝나고 하나 여쭤봐도 돼요?
May I ask one thing after class?
여쭤봐도 돼요 ('may I humbly ask') for after-class questions
nuance: 질문 있어요 is 질문 ('question', 質問) + 있어요 ('there is/I have'). It's the simple, correct way to signal you want to ask something. The polite upgrade for a teacher is the humble verb 여쭤보다 ('to ask (up)'), used when YOU ask a SUPERIOR: 여쭤봐도 돼요? ('may I ask?'). The key verb contrast English speakers must learn: 물어보다 is the plain 'to ask' (asking a peer or someone below you), while 여쭤보다 is its humble form for asking someone above you — using 물어봐도 돼요? to a respected teacher isn't wrong but 여쭤봐도 돼요? sounds more polished. A softer way to open is 질문 있는데요 (with -는데요, the gentle 'just so you know…' ender that invites the teacher to say 'go ahead'). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb 'have': don't say 질문 가지고 있어요 (직역 of 'have', sounds like physically holding a question) — Korean uses 있다 ('there is'): 질문 있어요.
